newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turk conservatives put polls pressure on Islamists.
newsitem.headline: Turk conservatives put polls pressure on Islamists.

text.p: The conservative wing of Turkey's governing coalition piled pressure on Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan on Thursday, giving its leader Tansu Ciller authority to bargain for early elections.
"We have established that the country is unmistakably in an election atmosphere," Foreign Minister Ciller told a news conference after a high-level meeting of her True Path Party.
She said she would tell Erbakan, modern Turkey's first Islamist leader, of her party's determination to go for polls. "We will share our thoughts and decisions with our partners," she said.
Erbakan and Ciller are to meet on Friday, aides said.

The 11-month-old alliance between Erbakan and pro-Western Ciller has been crumbling under pressure from the secularist establishment, which sees Erbakan's Welfare Party (RP) as the source of an Islamist revival in officially secular Turkey.
Ciller, a U.S.-trained economist, has already asked Erbakan to make her prime minister in a caretaker government that would take the country to the polls.

The two are set to swop jobs next year under a power-sharing deal that established their alliance last June. But Ciller says she can ward off anti-Islamist pressure on the government from the army if she takes the top job sooner.
A member of True Path's executive council, who declined to be named, told Reuters he believed this would happen.
"RP looks favourably on handing over the prime minister's job. The handover will take place soon. An election will be held within a year," he said.
But Welfare spokesman Salih Kapusuz said later it had made no decision to go to early elections or hand over power to Ciller.
"At the moment there is no definite result or decision on this issue," he told Reuters.

Shares in Istanbul were driven sharply lower by unconfirmed reports the coalition allies had agreed on the manoeuvres. The IMKB National-100 index was down 4.1 percent in late afternoon trading, but recovered to close down 2.3 percent on the day.
The leader of the main opposition Motherland Party poured scorn on the wrangling within the coalition.
"Whatever they are going to do, let them do it quickly," Anatolian news agency quoted Mesut Yilmaz as saying. "Turkey has never seen such a comedy before."
Yilmaz's party has vowed to bring a fresh censure motion against the government in early June.
The row over military-led demands for a crackdown on Islamist activism has already eroded the power of the alliance in parliament.
It narrowly survived the latest of a series of opposition censure motions in parliament last week. The desertion of several deputies has left it with a parliamentary majority of just one on paper.
A late bid to save the government from collapsing ran into trouble at a three-way meeting of party leaders on Wednesday.
Right-wing party leader Muhsin Yazicioglu said after the talks that he was reluctant to prop up the coalition until the alliance partners reached accord on the government's future.
The support of six deputies from Yazicioglu's party was crucial to the survival of the coalition at last week's censure motion.
Yazicioglu said Erbakan had so far rejected Ciller's call to make her prime minister until elections in spring 1998, two years before they are due.
"Ciller states that an early election atmosphere has been formed in Turkey. As for Erbakan, he says the government can continue until the year 2000," Yazicioglu said.

The political conflict has drawn domestic public attention away from Turkey's two-week-old anti-guerrilla operation against Kurdish rebels in northern Iraq, where Turkish troops consolidated their positions on Thursday.
More than 23,000 people have died in the armed struggle between Turkey's armed forces and the Kurdistan Workers Party which is in its 13th year.
